title: Vascular Diseases of the Kidney
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how disease of the renal vessels injures the kidney. It covers thrombotic microangiopathy (hemolytic uremic syndrome and its contrast with TTP), hypertensive arteriolar disease, renal artery stenosis, infarction, sickle cell injury to the medulla, and renal vein thrombosis. The kidney receives about 20% of cardiac output through end arteries and a medulla that runs close to hypoxia, so each vessel lesion produces a predictable pattern. Board items describe a blood smear, an arteriolar lesion, a gross kidney, or a bruit and ask you to predict blood pressure, renin, urine findings, and kidney size.
prerequisites: Renal arterial tree, end-artery supply, and the vasa recta (UR-2, UR-5)
Juxtaglomerular apparatus and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (UR-5, UR-7)
Hemostasis: platelets, von Willebrand factor, coagulation tests (PT, aPTT)
Hemoglobin S polymerization and the oxygen dissociation curve

connections.how: HUS, TTP, and sickle cell disease are blood disorders whose most important end-organ injury is in the kidney.
Hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, and endocarditis link heart and vessel disease to renal injury.
Nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy, creates the hypercoagulable state behind renal vein thrombosis.
Shiga toxin from enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 is the cause of typical HUS.

connections.to: Papillary necrosis and renal tumors (UR-12-D, UR-12-E)
connections.how: Sickle cell disease and trait cause papillary necrosis, and renal cell carcinoma can grow into the renal vein.

terms.def: Injury of small vessels with platelet or platelet-fibrin thrombi that narrow arterioles and capillaries, producing hemolysis and platelet consumption.
A fragmented red cell (helmet or triangle shape) formed when red cells are sheared by strands of fibrin or platelet thrombi in small vessels.
Intravascular hemolysis caused by mechanical fragmentation of red cells in damaged small vessels, with schistocytes on the smear and a negative direct Coombs test.
A plasma metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers; its deficiency causes TTP.
Homogeneous pink thickening of arteriolar walls from leaked plasma proteins and excess basement membrane matrix, typical of chronic hypertension, diabetes, and aging.
Concentric, laminated (onion-skin) thickening of arteriolar walls by proliferating smooth muscle cells and reduplicated basement membrane, typical of severe hypertension.
Necrosis of a vessel wall in which leaked plasma proteins and fibrin give a bright pink, smudgy appearance.
A noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic thickening of medium-sized artery walls that alternates with thin segments, giving a string of beads pattern.
A kidney rendered ischemic by renal artery narrowing, which secretes renin and causes renovascular hypertension.
An artery whose territory has no effective collateral supply, so its occlusion causes infarction of that territory.
Excretion of urine whose osmolality stays close to that of plasma (about 300 mOsm/kg) regardless of hydration, from loss of concentrating and diluting ability.
Ischemic necrosis of the renal papillary tips, which may slough into the collecting system.

sections.title: Hemolytic uremic syndrome and its contrast with TTP

blocks.text: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a thrombotic microangiopathy with a defining triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Typical HUS is a leading cause of acute kidney injury in young children. It follows bloody diarrhea from Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, most often serotype O157:H7, acquired from undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized milk or juice, contaminated produce, or person-to-person spread. Renal failure begins about 5 to 10 days after the diarrhea starts, often as the diarrhea is improving.
How Shiga toxin injures endothelium

Shiga toxin is an AB5 toxin. It does not need the bacteria to invade: it crosses the inflamed colonic mucosa into the blood. The five B subunits bind the glycolipid globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), which glomerular endothelial cells express in abundance, so the kidney bears the brunt. After uptake, the A subunit acts as an N-glycosidase that removes one adenine from the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit, halting protein synthesis. The injured endothelium swells, detaches, loses its anticoagulant surface, and releases ultra-large von Willebrand factor, so platelets adhere and platelet-fibrin thrombi form in glomerular capillaries and afferent arterioles.

blocks.title: From Shiga toxin to the HUS triad
steps: E. coli O157:H7 colitis causes bloody diarrhea
Shiga toxin enters the blood
B subunits bind Gb3 on glomerular endothelium
A subunit cleaves 28S rRNA; protein synthesis stops
Endothelial injury exposes a prothrombotic surface
Platelet-fibrin microthrombi narrow glomerular capillaries
Red cells are sheared into schistocytes; platelets are consumed
Glomerular filtration falls: acute kidney injury
blocks.caption: Endothelial injury is the starting point; hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure all follow from microthrombi in small renal vessels.

blocks.text: Each part of the triad follows from the microthrombi. Red cells forced through narrowed vessels are fragmented, producing schistocytes, a high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and a high reticulocyte count. Because the hemolysis is mechanical, the direct Coombs test is negative. Platelets are consumed in thrombi, but clotting factors are not consumed systemically, so PT and aPTT stay normal, which separates HUS and TTP from disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Occluded glomeruli cause oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, and azotemia.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) produces the same hemolysis and thrombocytopenia by a different route. ADAMTS13 normally trims ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers; when it is deficient, usually from an acquired autoantibody and rarely from inherited mutation, these multimers bind platelets spontaneously and form platelet-rich, fibrin-poor thrombi throughout the circulation. TTP mainly affects adults, especially women, and the brain is the dominant target, so confusion, headache, and focal deficits are common while renal injury is usually milder. Atypical HUS, a third form, results from uncontrolled alternative complement activation (for example factor H mutations) without diarrhea.

blocks.title: HUS, TTP, and DIC
blocks.caption: Normal clotting times point to a platelet-driven microangiopathy (HUS or TTP) rather than DIC; the patient and the dominant organ then separate HUS from TTP.

blocks.predict: A 4-year-old has pallor, petechiae, and low urine output a week after bloody diarrhea. Predict the smear, the direct Coombs test, and the PT.
blocks.explain: Schistocytes from mechanical shearing, a negative Coombs test because no antibody coats the red cells, and a normal PT because clotting factors are not consumed.

blocks.text: Hypertension damages the kidney through its arterioles, and the pattern depends on how high and how fast the pressure rises. The two lesions differ microscopically and grossly, and boards expect you to match each to its setting and its kidney.
Benign nephrosclerosis

Benign nephrosclerosis is the renal lesion of long-standing, moderately elevated pressure. Chronic hemodynamic stress injures arteriolar endothelium, plasma proteins seep into the wall, and smooth muscle cells lay down excess basement membrane matrix. The result is hyaline arteriolosclerosis: a homogeneous pink, glassy wall with a narrowed lumen. Larger interlobular and arcuate arteries show medial hypertrophy and intimal fibroelastic thickening. Because the narrowing is slow and diffuse, nephrons drop out patchily by ischemia: glomeruli collapse and sclerose, and their tubules atrophy and are replaced by fibrosis. Scattered scars pulled down between surviving nephrons give both kidneys a symmetric reduction in size with a finely granular surface and a thinned cortex. The usual clinical picture is mild proteinuria and slowly declining GFR. The same arteriolar lesion occurs with aging and diabetes, so hyaline arteriolosclerosis alone does not prove hypertension.
Malignant hypertension

Malignant hypertension is a severe, often abrupt rise in pressure, commonly with diastolic pressure above 120 mm Hg, accompanied by acute organ damage such as papilledema, retinal hemorrhages, encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury. It can arise on top of benign hypertension or secondary causes such as renal artery stenosis or systemic sclerosis. Two arteriolar lesions appear. Fibrinoid necrosis occurs when the wall gives way and fibrin and plasma proteins flood into it. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis develops as smooth muscle cells proliferate and lay down concentric layers of basement membrane, producing the onion-skin appearance that nearly occludes the lumen. Ruptured arterioles and capillaries bleed into the cortex, so the kidney surface shows pinpoint petechial hemorrhages: the flea-bitten kidney. Patients have rapidly rising creatinine, hematuria, and proteinuria, and endothelial damage can produce schistocytes and thrombocytopenia as a secondary microangiopathy.

blocks.title: The renin loop of malignant hypertension
steps: Severe pressure injures arteriolar endothelium
Fibrinoid necrosis and onion-skin narrowing
Glomeruli and juxtaglomerular cells become ischemic
Renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone rise sharply
Vasoconstriction and sodium retention raise pressure further
blocks.caption: Arteriolar narrowing makes the kidney behave as if it were underperfused, so renin release drives the pressure still higher.

blocks.title: Benign nephrosclerosis versus malignant hypertension
rows: Severe, rapid rise with acute organ damage
Normal or slightly small, petechial (flea-bitten) surface
blocks.caption: The words hyaline and granular signal chronic disease; onion skin, fibrinoid necrosis, and flea-bitten signal an emergency.

sections.title: Renal artery stenosis and renovascular hypertension

blocks.text: Renal artery stenosis causes only a small share of hypertension (about 2 to 5%), but it matters because it is potentially curable. Two lesions account for nearly all cases. Atherosclerosis, responsible for about two thirds or more, affects older adults with the usual vascular risk factors (smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, other atherosclerotic disease); the plaque sits at the ostium or the proximal third of the artery, often as an extension of aortic plaque. Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) affects mainly women under about 50. It is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic thickening of the arterial wall, most often of the media, that alternates with thinned segments, producing a string of beads pattern in the middle and distal artery on angiography. FMD can involve the carotid and vertebral arteries as well.

blocks.title: Atherosclerotic stenosis versus fibromuscular dysplasia
rows: Older adult with vascular risk factors
Mid to distal artery, sometimes bilateral
Fibrous and muscular wall thickening, usually medial
Often found as new hypertension in a young patient
blocks.caption: Age, sex, and the position of the narrowing separate the two causes.

blocks.text: Why stenosis raises blood pressure

The juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole act as intrarenal baroreceptors. A stenosis lowers perfusion pressure beyond it, so they release renin even though systemic pressure is normal or high. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles throughout the body, and aldosterone retains sodium and water, which raises pressure. Aldosterone also increases potassium and hydrogen secretion in the collecting duct, so some patients have hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis (secondary hyperaldosteronism, with high renin and high aldosterone). Turbulent flow across the narrowed lumen produces a systolic or continuous bruit over the abdomen or flank.

blocks.title: Renovascular hypertension
steps: Stenosis lowers afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure
Juxtaglomerular cells release renin
Angiotensin II constricts systemic arterioles
Aldosterone retains sodium; secretes potassium and hydrogen ions
Systemic hypertension, sometimes with hypokalemia
blocks.caption: The stenotic kidney reads its low perfusion as low body volume and defends a pressure that the rest of the body does not need.

blocks.text: The two kidneys then age differently. The stenotic kidney is shielded from the high systemic pressure but chronically underperfused, so its tubules atrophy and it shrinks (ischemic atrophy); a size difference between the kidneys is a clue. The opposite kidney receives the full hypertensive pressure and develops arteriolosclerosis. In the affected kidney, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, which holds glomerular capillary pressure and GFR up despite low inflow. Blocking angiotensin II formation removes that support.

blocks.title: Worked example: a rise in creatinine after an ACE inhibitor
blocks.text: A 70-year-old smoker with resistant hypertension and an abdominal bruit starts an ACE inhibitor, and his creatinine rises from 1.2 to 2.0 mg/dL. Reason it through. GFR depends on glomerular capillary pressure, which sits between afferent inflow and efferent outflow resistance. With proximal stenosis, inflow pressure is low, and the kidney preserves filtration by letting angiotensin II constrict the efferent arteriole. The ACE inhibitor removes angiotensin II, the efferent arteriole relaxes, glomerular pressure falls, and GFR drops. If only one kidney is stenotic, the healthy kidney usually compensates. A sharp rise in creatinine therefore suggests bilateral stenosis or stenosis of a solitary functioning kidney.

The renal artery divides into segmental, interlobar, arcuate, and interlobular arteries, and these branches behave as end arteries with no useful collateral flow between them. Occlusion of a branch therefore kills the whole territory it supplies. Because the kidney is a solid organ with a single arterial supply, the dead tissue undergoes coagulative necrosis: cell outlines persist while nuclei disappear, and little blood enters the dead zone, so the infarct is pale (anemic) rather than hemorrhagic. The vessels fan outward from the hilum, so the infarct is wedge-shaped, with its base at the capsule and its apex pointing toward the hilum. Early on, a red hyperemic rim surrounds the pale zone. Over weeks, the necrotic tissue is replaced by fibrous scar, leaving a depressed V-shaped cortical scar.

Most renal infarcts are embolic. The kidneys receive about 20% of cardiac output straight from the aorta, so thrombi from the left heart reach them easily. The main sources are left atrial thrombi in atrial fibrillation, left ventricular mural thrombi after a myocardial infarction or in dilated cardiomyopathy, and vegetations of infective endocarditis (septic emboli can also cause abscesses). Less often the artery thromboses in place, over an atherosclerotic plaque, after aortic or renal artery dissection or trauma, or in a hypercoagulable state.

Clinically, many small infarcts are silent. A larger one causes sudden flank or abdominal pain, nausea, fever, and hematuria, sometimes with a sudden rise in blood pressure from renin released by the ischemic margin. Serum LDH rises from the dead tissue, which helps distinguish infarction from kidney stones, a common mimic. Renal function falls substantially only when both kidneys or a solitary kidney are affected.

Atheroembolic renal disease is a separate entity. Cholesterol crystals released from ulcerated aortic plaque, often after angiography or aortic surgery, lodge in many small arcuate and interlobular arteries. They leave needle-shaped clefts in the vessels, cause many tiny infarcts and a slow decline in GFR, and are often accompanied by livedo reticularis and transient eosinophilia rather than a single wedge.

Hemoglobin S (HbS) differs from hemoglobin A by a single substitution, valine for glutamate at position 6 of the beta chain. Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into long fibers that distort the red cell, and the delay before polymerization shortens steeply as the HbS concentration rises. Sickling is therefore favored by low oxygen, red cell dehydration (which concentrates HbS), and low pH (which, through the Bohr effect, lowers oxygen affinity and increases the deoxygenated fraction). The renal medulla supplies all three at once.

Countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta lets oxygen diffuse from descending to ascending vessels, so the inner medulla has a low oxygen tension even in health. Its interstitium is strongly hypertonic, reaching about 1,200 mOsm/kg in maximally concentrated states, which draws water out of red cells. Accumulated CO2 and acid keep the pH low. Blood also moves slowly through the long vasa recta, giving polymers time to form. Sickled cells occlude the vasa recta and cause microinfarcts in the medulla and papillae.

blocks.title: Why the medulla sickles
steps: Countercurrent exchange keeps medullary oxygen low
Hypertonic interstitium dehydrates red cells, concentrating HbS
Low pH lowers oxygen affinity (Bohr effect)
Slow vasa recta flow allows polymerization
Sickled cells occlude vasa recta
Medullary microinfarcts and papillary necrosis
blocks.caption: The features that let the medulla concentrate urine are the same ones that make it the ideal place for HbS to sickle.

blocks.text: The consequences follow from what the medulla does. Loss of vasa recta and of the deep loops of Henle destroys the countercurrent gradient, so the urine can no longer be concentrated much above plasma. This defect usually appears in childhood and produces isosthenuria (urine near 300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity about 1.010), polyuria, nocturia, enuresis, and a heightened risk of dehydration, which in turn promotes more sickling. Ischemic papillae can necrose and slough, causing hematuria, colicky pain, or ureteral obstruction. Painless gross or microscopic hematuria from medullary microinfarcts is common, and it occurs more often from the left kidney. Distal tubular dysfunction can impair potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.

Sickle cell trait (HbAS) carries enough HbS, about 35 to 40%, to sickle under the extreme medullary conditions even though trait carriers are not anemic and rarely sickle elsewhere. Hematuria, a mild concentrating defect, and papillary necrosis therefore occur in trait as well as in disease. Trait is also associated with renal medullary carcinoma, a rare, aggressive tumor of young people. In sickle cell disease (HbSS), anemia also drives cortical hyperfiltration, which over years leads to proteinuria and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

blocks.predict: A 19-year-old athlete with sickle cell trait has painless hematuria and cannot concentrate urine after overnight water restriction. Why does trait injure the kidney when it spares other organs?
blocks.explain: Only the medulla combines low oxygen, high osmolality, and low pH with slow flow, which together push the modest HbS fraction in trait red cells to polymerize.

blocks.text: Renal vein thrombosis follows Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Nephrotic syndrome supplies hypercoagulability and infant dehydration supplies stasis. Renal cell carcinoma deserves special mention because, unlike most tumors, it characteristically grows as a solid tumor thrombus along the renal vein, sometimes extending through the inferior vena cava into the right atrium.

blocks.title: Causes of renal vein thrombosis
rows: Hypercoagulability from urinary loss of antithrombin and increased hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and other clotting factors
Tumor grows directly into the renal vein and may extend into the inferior vena cava; tumor and attached thrombus obstruct flow
Hemoconcentration and low renal venous flow (stasis); risk is higher in infants of diabetic mothers
Trauma, extrinsic compression, oral contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias
blocks.caption: Nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause in adults, and membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk among nephrotic diseases.

blocks.text: Nephrotic syndrome is hypercoagulable for several reasons. Antithrombin is a small protein, about the size of albumin, so it leaks through the damaged filtration barrier and its plasma level falls. The liver responds to low plasma oncotic pressure by increasing synthesis of many proteins, including fibrinogen and factors V and VIII, which are too large to be lost in the urine. Platelet aggregability increases, and intravascular volume depletion adds hemoconcentration. The risk rises as serum albumin falls. Why membranous nephropathy carries a higher risk than other nephrotic lesions is not fully explained.

blocks.title: From renal vein occlusion to the clinical picture
steps: Thrombus blocks renal venous outflow
Back pressure congests peritubular and glomerular capillaries
Kidney swells with edema and hemorrhage
Congested glomeruli leak more blood and protein
Flank pain, hematuria, rising proteinuria, enlarged kidney
blocks.caption: Venous obstruction enlarges the kidney, the opposite of arterial disease, which shrinks it.

blocks.text: Acute, complete occlusion causes sudden flank pain, gross hematuria, an enlarged and sometimes palpable kidney, a rise in proteinuria, and a fall in GFR, which is severe when both veins are involved. In a neonate the triad is a flank mass, hematuria, and thrombocytopenia. Gradual occlusion in an adult is often silent because collateral veins (capsular, ureteric, and on the left side gonadal and adrenal) develop, and it may be discovered only after a pulmonary embolism. The left renal vein receives the left gonadal vein, so left renal vein obstruction, by thrombus or by renal cell carcinoma, raises pressure in the left pampiniform plexus and can cause a new left varicocele that does not empty when the patient lies down.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain why vessel disease is so damaging here. End arteries make every branch occlusion a complete infarct, the afferent arteriole holds the renin sensor that turns stenosis and arteriolar narrowing into systemic hypertension, and the countercurrent design that concentrates urine also keeps the medulla hypoxic, hypertonic, and acidic, which is why HbS sickles there. The direction of the lesion predicts kidney size: arterial narrowing shrinks the kidney by ischemic atrophy, while venous obstruction swells it with congestion.

Microbiology, biochemistry, immunology, and pathology meet in the microangiopathies. A bacterial toxin that cleaves rRNA (HUS), an autoantibody against a protease (TTP), complement dysregulation (atypical HUS), and severe hypertension all converge on endothelial injury with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia, and normal clotting times separate them from DIC. These distinctions have limits: malignant hypertension and systemic sclerosis can also produce a secondary microangiopathy, so the setting and the organ pattern must be read together with the smear.

summary: Typical HUS follows E. coli O157:H7 colitis in a child: Shiga toxin binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelium, cleaves 28S rRNA, and triggers platelet-fibrin microthrombi.
The triad of HUS and TTP is schistocytes with negative Coombs test, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury, with normal PT and aPTT, unlike DIC.
TTP results from ADAMTS13 deficiency and ultra-large vWF multimers, affects mainly adults, and injures the brain more than the kidney.

Benign nephrosclerosis shows hyaline arteriolosclerosis and symmetric, finely granular small kidneys; malignant hypertension shows onion-skin arteriolosclerosis, fibrinoid necrosis, a flea-bitten kidney, and acute kidney injury.
Renal artery stenosis raises renin through low afferent perfusion: atherosclerosis at the ostium in older adults, fibromuscular dysplasia with a string of beads in young women.
The stenotic kidney shrinks, depends on angiotensin II efferent constriction to maintain GFR, and the opposite kidney develops arteriolosclerosis.
Renal infarcts are usually embolic from the left heart and appear as pale, wedge-shaped coagulative necrosis with flank pain, hematuria, and high LDH.
Low oxygen, high osmolality, low pH, and slow flow make the medulla sickle, causing isosthenuria, hematuria, and papillary necrosis in disease and trait.
Renal vein thrombosis complicates nephrotic syndrome (especially membranous), renal cell carcinoma, and infant dehydration, and enlarges the kidney with flank pain and hematuria.

verify: Timing of HUS after diarrhea onset (about 5 to 10 days) and the share of children with O157:H7 infection who develop HUS vary between sources.

Threshold for malignant hypertension: this chapter says commonly diastolic above 120 mm Hg; sources also quote 180/120 or 200/120 mm Hg, and current guidelines use the term hypertensive emergency. Confirm the wording NABNE uses.
Renal artery stenosis share of hypertension (about 2 to 5%), proportion due to atherosclerosis (about two thirds to 90%), and the age range for fibromuscular dysplasia differ between texts.
The statement that sickle cell hematuria arises more often from the left kidney is classic in review texts, but the mechanism is not established; confirm whether NABNE tests it.
HbS fraction in sickle cell trait (about 35 to 40%) and the peak medullary osmolality (about 1,200 mOsm/kg) are approximate consensus values.
Renal vein thrombosis with renal cell carcinoma and the left varicocele sign are USMLE-extension content (UR-12-F.6 is not one of the listed NPLEX conditions); confirm coverage depth.
